[0m[1m[2m[48;2;51;51;60m› [0m[48;2;51;51;60mAgain without tools: write two long paragraphs of plain prose, at least 100 words each, about why  [0m
[0m[48;2;51;51;60m  pane widths in a terminal multiplexer can differ from what a layout engine reports.                [0m
[0m[48;2;51;51;60m                                                                                                     [0m
 
[0m[2m• [0mPane widths in a terminal multiplexer can differ from what a layout engine reports because the two
  measurements may describe different boundaries. A layout engine might report the rectangle
  allocated to a pane, while the multiplexer exposes only the columns available for terminal content
  inside that rectangle. Borders, separators, padding, and reserved interface elements can consume
  part of the allocation. Another source of disagreement is converting proportional layouts into
  whole character cells. If three panes share a width that cannot be divided evenly, the layout must
  assign the remaining columns somewhere, and different calculations may distribute those columns
  differently. A parent layout might also report coordinates relative to the entire window, while a
  child measures its own content region. Comparing those values without accounting for their origins
  and whether their endpoints are inclusive can produce a consistent discrepancy of one or more
  columns.
 
  The reported widths can also describe different moments in a resize operation. A layout engine may
  calculate a new pane arrangement before the multiplexer updates the pane’s pseudo-terminal size, or
  an application may retain its previous dimensions until it processes a resize notification. During
  that interval, each component can report a reasonable value that belongs to a different state.
  Nested multiplexers and remote connections add more stages where dimensions can be delayed,
  constrained, or inherited from another session. A multiplexer may also maintain a logical window
  size that differs from the currently visible client area, depending on how attached clients and
  window sizing policies are handled. Finally, a layout engine that measures pixels must translate
  those measurements into terminal columns, introducing rounding and assumptions about cell size. To
  understand a mismatch, the useful comparison is between measurements taken at the same time, in the
  same units, and for the same content boundary.
